title: Contribution documentation + optional pre-commit hook
body:
# Overview
I've added an (optional) pre-commit hook that can be installed via:
```shell
pip install pre-commit
pre-commit install
```
Assuming you have some version of python/pip installed and available on your path.

This adds a pre-commit hook that will automatically install CSharpier if it isn't installed and run it on changed files. It will reject the commit if there are any formatting diffs, and update the current staged files to be the correctly formatted files

Here's an example of me running it after adding a trailing space in `CharData`:
```powershell
D:\Code\DxMessaging-Unity\Packages\TextTween [dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier*]
λ» git status
On branch dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   .config/dotnet-tools.json
        modified:   Runtime/CharData.cs

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   Runtime/CharData.cs


D:\Code\DxMessaging-Unity\Packages\TextTween [dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier*]
λ» git add --all

D:\Code\DxMessaging-Unity\Packages\TextTween [dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier*]
λ» git commit -m "Pre-commit test"
Install .NET tools.......................................................Passed
Run CSharpier on C# files................................................Failed
- hook id: csharpier
- files were modified by this hook

Formatted 1 files in 153ms.

D:\Code\DxMessaging-Unity\Packages\TextTween [dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier*]
λ» git status
On branch dev/wallstop/pre-commit-csharpier
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   .config/dotnet-tools.json
        modified:   Runtime/CharData.cs

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   Runtime/CharData.cs
```

Maybe what isn't clear here is that, after I tried to run `git commit`, it ran CSharpier and properly formatted the file, then left it in my staging area for me to decide if it's a change I want.

If you enable this, you no longer have to worry about whether or not you have CSharpier installed or if you're actively running it or whatever, it'll run automatically when you go to check in!

Added some brief documentation about CSharpier usage as well as a link to the installation documentation for `pre-commit`.
author: wallstop

title: Fix text addition / removal bug (#28)
body:
# Overview
See #28 for the issue

# The Fix (Fixes #28, Fixes #5)
I've done five things here:
1. Cached a reference to `OnTextChanged` such that we're not re-creating new delegates on every OnEnable/OnDisable call
2. Keep stateful knowledge of whether this delegate is attached
3. Update `OnTextChanged` to not call `UpdateMeshes`. This allows for safe addition, removal, and automatic re-calculation of the meshes
4. Changed ApplyModifiers to not throw. This is important - TweenManager may be initialized early than the text meshes. The hook into the TEXT_CHANGED_EVENT will be triggered when the text meshes are safely initialized.
5. Changed ForceMeshUpdate to only happen in non-PlayMode. I was having issues related to this in Play mode - I think if it's in Play Mode, things will initialize naturally.

Now, I edit text while the editor isn't playing and have it behave expectedly, AND I can do the same in play mode.
author: wallstop

comments.body:
This works great with single texts but when there are multiple texts, since the unchanged text mesh is not regenerated, the changes get reapplied.

### Reproduction
1.  Add multiple texts to TweenManger
2. Set progress above 0 so there are changes to apply
3. Start changing one of the texts

> This works great with single texts but when there are multiple texts, since the unchanged text mesh is not regenerated, the changes get reapplied.
> ### Reproduction
> 
>     1. Add multiple texts to TweenManger
> 
>     2. Set progress above 0 so there are changes to apply
> 
>     3. Start changing one of the texts

Great catch and thanks for the repro. I believe I've fixed this as well as some related bugs due to text changing.

Here's what I've done:
1. Added some stateful knowledge about text -> last known vertex count. When handling multiple texts within a single TweenManager, we still want to restore the meshes of texts that are *not* the current one. However, since they're all stored in a giant array and we don't know what our "current" value of allocated space within that array is (due to all knowledge of "size" being current state, not state when the array was computed), this was needed. The concept is pretty simple - on init, cache text -> vertex count, such that we know which texts are using what size in our buffer. On Dispose, clear the cache. On text change, if the text being changed is in the cache, do not update its mesh, but advance the pointer in our buffer by the appropriate (cached, not current) value.
2. Fixed a bug related to visible character count. To test this I created several texts and added/removed characters from them. When adding characters, everything worked as expected. However, when removing characters, things were not working as expected. I found out that the current TMP impl does some optimizations related to array resizing. That is, on character removal, it doesn't do anything to character data in the `text.textInfo.characterInfo` array - it keeps the old state there, *including* the `isVisible` property (!!!). What it *does* do, though, is expose a `characterCount` property, which appears to accurately reflect the state of "which character data is accurate". I had to update this in two places - the GetVisibleCharCount method as well as in CreateCharDataArray that calls it
3. Fixed a bug where I forgot to set _eventAdded=true when we add the event, resulting in a listener leak.

title: Add Performance Tests (Fixes #19)
body:
# Overview
Using the job system is great, and might very well be extremely performant. However, just using the job framework does not guarantee performance. There is the cost of marshaling from current state to buffers the job framework uses, then the cost of splitting out the work, then the cost of  marshaling the job framework data back to the text arrays.

I have several ideas about how to improve performance, but without benchmarks, you can't really say whether or not one idea is faster than another. Data doesn't lie 😎. The first step towards more perf is having data about the current state of the world.

# The Fix (Fixes #19)
I've done a few things here, all in service of having meaningful performance benchmarks.
✓ Migrated reflected fields to public/private access gated on whether or not you're in Unity Editor. This adds some safety and allows tests and editor scripts to modify state, which is needed. I understand that modifying these at runtime poses challenges (as you need to recompute buffers/state). Am open to alternatives, but this is a pattern that I've had success with in other projects.
✓ Added some simple performance tests that run modifiers across different inputs. I chose the input sequence of "A" repeated some number of times. "A" has an "interesting" number of vertices.
✓ I've changed all of the properties on existing CharModifier implementations to be public (with back-compat serialization attributes, so as not to break existing users). I don't see a reason to hide these, it can be useful to set these up programmatically (like I need to do in tests) and modifying the properties at runtime poses no issue, as all of the job system work is currently blocked on the main thread. There is no time in which the job framework does not have a consistent view of the various bits of state.
✓ Fixed several inconsistencies in null checks for texts in TweenManager - some loops were doing this, some were not
✓ Fixed a bug where removing the last text instance from a TweenManager would throw an exception
✓ Fixed a bug where empty text would throw
✓ Moved (most) usings of changed files into inside namespace - this has the highest chance of not breaking users. When usings are outside of the namespace, depending on how things are named, this has the potential to break client code.
✓ Added current benchmarks to README. The benchmark tests are structured in such a way that you can just copy-paste the output from Unity's Test Runner into the README and it'll be a valid markdown table.

# Ideas for Perf Improvement
Note: All of these need testing

1. See how fast a simple for loop is. It might be faster to just for loop over stuff if the size of the data is less than some threshold.
2. Change batch size from 64 to some other number (dynamically?)
3. Instead of generating temp arrays every call, cache persistent arrays and just memcpy data to them

# PR Feedback
If the above changes are too much to review/take all at once, but you're interested in taking some/all of them, I can break this PR up into smaller ones and stage them however you see fit, just let me know!
Also, I'm running CSharpier with default settings, if you have settings like a different line length or whatever, I can try to figure out how to set things up such that the config is checked into the repo and available for all contributors.

Previous code seems to be built towards the assumption that there was only 1 text, which already has similar short-circuits built in.

title: Add using statements to ensure no memory leaks
body:
# Overview
Currently, if there is an exception in `UpdateMeshes`, which is possible as there's a lot of direct indexing and math going on, the `vertices` and `colors` temporary native arrays will not be disposed, leading to potentially (multiple) memory leaks.

# The fix (fixes #18)
For all types that implement `IDisposable`, C# lets you create `using` statements upon declaration.  When doing so, IL is generated in such a way that the `Dispose` method on each variable is called deterministically on scope exit, regardless of exceptional circumstances or whatever. This allows for very clean and framework-supported solution to this problem.

# Tips and tricks
In general, whenever you have a variable that implements IDisposable that you both create and call Dispose on in the same scope, prefer `using` instead to ensure your variable is always disposed.

title: Fix Dragging + Dropping in Editor
body:
# Overview
With the current Editor script, I am unable to drag + drop modifiers or text into the Texts/Modifiers lists. The only way I am able to add items is by clicking "+" and then dragging / selecting items from there. The main way I populate these items is by dragging + dropping in editor, this breaks my workflow.

# The Fix
Instead of doing fancy serialized property checks / wizardy / custom application, I've changed the Editor code to just draw and do the normal serialization things. All of the "is this different?" code has been moved to explicit state management, which solves this particular bug. 

# Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a Tween Manager
2. Create a TMP Text instance somewhere
3. Create a Modifier somewhere
4. Try dragging either the Text or Modifier into the Texts/Modifiers fields

Expected results: Dragged Text/Modifiers are added

Actual results: Nothing happens

# Extra Info
OS: Windows 11
Unity: 2022.3.51f1
author: wallstop

title: Not Proper Resetting when values change
body:
When things change, either text contents, vertex count, whatever, the TweenManager needs to reset that text state back to its initial value before updating its buffers.

Right now, things are re-initialized from *current* state, not *initial* state. That means that, if things are modified at runtime, you will end up with corrupted state.
